33e1d7779a:81005b278cd61d65.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
33e1d7779a:81005b278cd61d65.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:81005b278cd61d65.summary: Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyper-polarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum. Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI , is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale. Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting . The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah) . The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging: Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock. Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar. The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews. Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout. State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas…

33e1d7779a:d9912477397a3d72.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
33e1d7779a:d9912477397a3d72.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:d9912477397a3d72.summary: Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone. Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality. Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns. While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period. More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace. Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030. Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multi-day selloff of its stock and debt. Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf. Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue. It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times . Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on…

33e1d7779a:37a079dab1293844.title: Trump's MAGA allies openly discuss martial law
33e1d7779a:37a079dab1293844.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:37a079dab1293844.summary: MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged." Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president. Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence. Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June . Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment. Zoom in: On a September 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies. Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios. Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment. Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible. "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have." State of play:…

33e1d7779a:fe59e7311ded5d89.title: "Oh, shut up": Maine Senate debate gets testy
33e1d7779a:fe59e7311ded5d89.author: Mike Zapler
33e1d7779a:fe59e7311ded5d89.summary: Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson were sparring in a testy debate Thursday night when a protester loudly interrupted them. "So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said. "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." Why it matters: Collins and Jackson are competing in one of a handful of races that will determine the Senate majority. The two have traded barbs in a series of tense debates, but this was the first time they sounded like children arguing on a playground. Zoom in : At another point in the debate, Collins, who's been accused of not standing up to President Trump enough, was asked by a moderator to name a time when she opposed him and it changed the outcome. "At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth," she responded, referring to the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation. "As you undoubtedly have read, at the very last minute one of our Republicans changed his mind. Otherwise he would've been defeated for that job." Collins was talking about Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who went on to call his eventual decision to vote for Hegseth the "biggest regret of my career." "So that didn't change the outcome," the moderator said.

33e1d7779a:68702258f95157a1.title: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
33e1d7779a:68702258f95157a1.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:68702258f95157a1.summary: President Trump is preemptively blaming Sen. John Cornyn and Karl Rove for "doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton" to win the Texas Senate race. Why it matters: The president is publicly spinning what would be a disaster for Republicans on election night. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. "If Ken Paxton loses , it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove," Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump won Texas by 14 points just two years ago. What to watch: Trump's post comes the same day FEC campaign finance reports confirmed Elon Musk's efforts to help Paxton across the finish line. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September over two transactions, as Axios reported Thursday morning . The day after each Musk donation , SLF made an equal-sized transfer to a Texas PAC— a pop-up super PAC dedicated to electing Paxton. The big picture: A new poll this week in Texas showed Democrat James Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton, 50% to 47%. Republican leaders warned Trump for months that if Paxton won the primary against Cornyn it would be cost the party far more to keep the seat. Those predictions are proving true, with more than $500 million in ad spending already flowing into the Texas Senate race, according to AdImpact. "Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs," Cornyn told Semafor earlier in October after audio leaked from a Paxton event in D.C. The other side: Talarico is getting pummeled with some of that money, but he's far from defenseless. He was already on the air in August, when Paxton and Republicans were still figuring out their game plan — and who would foot the bill. Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter off an army of small donors. His campaign said 97% of contributions were under $100. Talarico's fundraising prowess allowed him to raise hard dollars, which command lower ad rates. "Oh my god, holy crap, I saw Talarico,"…

33e1d7779a:83cae9de5d44b6b5.title: GOP senator: Cancel Thanksgiving recess if we lose
33e1d7779a:83cae9de5d44b6b5.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:83cae9de5d44b6b5.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno wants his fellow Republicans to cancel their holiday plans and jam through "everything that we could possibly get" if they lose the majorities in November's midterms. Why it matters: Republicans couldn't muster the votes for a megabill this summer, and leadership is not confident they can now. But Moreno (R-Ohio) is calling for the GOP to make a bigger push in the event of losing power. "We will do a reconciliation bill, one way or the other," Moreno — who said it is "more likely" the GOP holds the Senate — told reporters outside the Capitol on Thursday. But if Republicans lose: "It'll be the 'Last Supper.' So it'll be a giant reconciliation bill where we take all the Republican priorities that we can get done." "If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all," he said. "Like, we'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving." Zoom in: Conversations have been ongoing in congressional offices about what a reconciliation package might look like in the lame-duck session between the election and the new Congress next year, a source familiar with the matter tells Axios. "We are working with the House and White House to develop what all is included to be able to sell to the public and our Republican colleagues when we return," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Budget Committee, told Axios. Election outcomes won't substantively change much for frequent holdouts like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) who are on their way out. That's not to mention Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), who are appropriators and known to break from the party. What to watch: Republicans face a long to-do list in the lame-duck, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and raising the debt ceiling. Those could all be considered part of a massive reconciliation package that requires just a…

33e1d7779a:5589a2d198d93919.title: Rubio urges Lebanon to resist Hezbollah pressure over seized explosives
33e1d7779a:5589a2d198d93919.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:5589a2d198d93919.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio pressed Lebanon President Joseph Aoun not to return to Hezbollah a truck full of explosives it attempted to smuggle into Beirut several days ago, according to a State Department official and another source with knowledge of the call. Why it matters: The issue is a test case for the Lebanese government's resolve to stand up to Hezbollah and implement its policy of keeping weapons outside the control of state security forces. Driving the news: Lebanese security forces intercepted the truck last week at a checkpoint on the highway connecting the Bekaa Valley to Beirut. The truck was carrying approximately 780 kilograms of explosives, including TNT and C-4, Lebanese officials said. Two suspects were arrested for transporting the shipment. After the arrest , Hezbollah acknowledged that the explosives belonged to them but claimed they were intended for use against the Israeli military in southern Lebanon. Hezbollah's opponents in Lebanon seized on the incident as further proof of the danger of the Shia militia's weapons and its independent military activity. Hezbollah and its allies in Lebanon have since pressed the government to release its two members and return the explosives to the militia. Behind the scenes: The State Department official said Rubio urged Aoun to "hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question." Aoun assured Rubio that the Lebanese army and security forces are fully implementing decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the president's office said. Aoun also stressed that the judicial authorities will show no leniency toward those responsible and will enforce the laws without favoritism. "No one will be released unless he is innocent," Aoun told Rubio according to a Lebanese official. The big picture: Rubio also raised Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which…

33e1d7779a:c0989f8802f79d5b.title: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots
33e1d7779a:c0989f8802f79d5b.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:c0989f8802f79d5b.summary: The Trump administration is suing California and two election officials over claims that there are suspected ineligible voters who received mail-in ballots for this November's election . Why it matters: The lawsuit is asking the court to prevent about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted until their citizenship status is confirmed. What they're saying: "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release statement. "If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government," Blanche said. Zoom in: The Justice Department alleges that California is knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote in the federal elections, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and ICE's investigative arm compiled the list of potentially ineligible voters using agency data and records from the Social Security Administration and State Department. But administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on the voter rolls have been found less than accurate before in Nevada , Pennsylvania and New Jersey . Zoom out: California's top election official and Los Angeles County's election chief received letters two days ago threatening "emergency action." The Justice Department gave Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan a password-protected thumb drive listing more than 20,000 voters and instructed him to verify their citizenship within 48 hours, according to the department's letter and statements. "Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office. Our response will be grounded in compliance with federal and state voter registration laws and procedures," Logan said in a statement on social media after the initial letter. Friction point: Federal law…

33e1d7779a:8990c7e1917ae00c.title: Fired FBI agents sue Kash Patel to get jobs back
33e1d7779a:8990c7e1917ae00c.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:8990c7e1917ae00c.summary: Nine former FBI agents and intelligence personnel sued the Trump administration Thursday, alleging they were unlawfully fired for working on the investigation into President Trump's handling of classified documents . Why it matters: The agents' bid to regain their jobs adds to a growing number of legal challenges accusing the Trump administration of retaliating against FBI personnel who investigated the president. Driving the news: "Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the 70-page lawsuit says. "As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs' investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts. The impact of these heedless actions on America's national security is immeasurable." All nine plaintiffs are seeking their jobs back. FBI Director Kash Patel , Attorney General Todd Blanche and their agencies are named as defendants. The other side: Patel said in February termination letters that the employees had "exercised poor judgment and a lack of impartiality in carrying out duties, leading to the political weaponization of the government," according to the lawsuit. The FBI did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the lawsuit. Zoom in: The lawsuit disputes Patel's accusations, saying none of the plaintiffs had any history of "misconduct or poor behavior while employed with the FBI." None had been internally investigated for wrongdoing, nor were they given the opportunity to explain or appeal their terminations. The lawsuit alleges the firings bypassed FBI policy requiring an administrative inquiry before disciplinary action. The complaint also notes that "[i]n many instances, Plaintiffs' immediate supervisors expressed disbelief and regret that Plaintiffs' FBI careers had been ended." What they're saying: "With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our…

33e1d7779a:167fa4d89967a91c.title: "Mommy and daddy" play nice: Apple and Meta team up to bring open-source Muse to Macs
33e1d7779a:167fa4d89967a91c.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:167fa4d89967a91c.summary: Apple and Meta, whose leaders have spent years trading barbs over privacy and the future of computing, are joining forces to bring one of America's most powerful open-weight AI models to Apple's high-end Macs. Why it matters: The collaboration marks a striking détente between two longtime Silicon Valley rivals, underscoring how the AI race is reshaping relationships across the technology industry. The companies still compete over devices and the next generation of computing, but both see an opportunity in bringing powerful AI capabilities to personal computers. "We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again," Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios. Driving the news: Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open, a model similar to Muse Spark 1.3, that it says is the most powerful U.S.-developed open-weight AI model available. Meta joins a host of Western AI companies that have released powerful open-weight systems that promise to slash AI costs, provide companies with more control and offer an alternative to the Chinese AI ecosystem. Nvidia on Tuesday released updated versions of its Nemotron family of models, and U.S.-based Reflection AI and France's Mistral both released new open source models last week. As proof of Muse Spark Open's capabilities, Meta worked with Apple to make the model run locally across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework. Zoom in : The prospect of a powerful model — it has 816 billion parameters — running on Apple hardware offers a proof of concept about just how much companies will be able to build their own AI systems. That could give companies more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs and proprietary models from leading AI labs, potentially shifting some of the economics of AI. Meta's model will be free to download, with a license allowing commercial use, and will also be available through cloud providers and developer tools. What they're saying: Wang said the companies have been…

33e1d7779a:b36cec5551547788.title: The too-hot-for-comfort economy
33e1d7779a:b36cec5551547788.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:b36cec5551547788.summary: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply. The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction. There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response. Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday. Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher. There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows. Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years. If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy. State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28. Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month. Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that…

33e1d7779a:70907431e33d22ec.title: America's wits' end election approaches
33e1d7779a:70907431e33d22ec.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:70907431e33d22ec.summary: Data: AP-NORC; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios A quartet of polls out this week carry a stark message: Americans feel disgruntled, dizzy and down on the man in the White House. Why it matters: The vibes going into the midterms are bleak, with a large majority of voters wanting significant change. But the question remains whether those sentiments will drive them to the polls. Driving the news: Nearly two-thirds of Americans rate the economy negatively, per a Fox News poll out Wednesday. Seven in ten voters say they feel like things in the country are out of control, per a The Economist/YouGov survey conducted October 10-12. And eight in ten, new AP/NORC polling found, want to see either "substantial change" or "complete and total upheaval" in how the country is run. Among Republicans, 58% share those sentiments. Zoom out: That national angst appears to be dragging down the president's approval. Fox News found that Trump's approval rating on inflation, which picked up last month, is at a new low: 22%. His overall job approval rating has also fallen to a new floor in Fox News surveys for either term: 36%. Fox says that drop is largely driven by voters under 45, those with household incomes below $50,000, non-white voters and those without a college degree. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Yes, but: Polling suggests that disgruntlement doesn't necessarily translate into a wellspring of positive energy toward Democrats. Far more voters say they're somewhat or very pessimistic about the Democratic Party's future (47%) than those who say they're optimistic (21%), per AP/NORC. About half say they're pessimistic about Republicans' future, while around 23% say they're optimistic. Still, Fox found that if the election were held today, 54% of voters would back the Democrat in their House district, while 45% would support the Republican — a wider lead for Dems than the prior month. Plus, Fox found that Republicans have lost ground to Democrats…

33e1d7779a:e037400fd84d8496.title: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed
33e1d7779a:e037400fd84d8496.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e037400fd84d8496.summary: President Trump said in a Thursday Truth Social post the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter by firing squad will not be live-streamed. The big picture: The president's post walks back an idea that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched last week, setting off an avalanche of bipartisan condemnation. Driving the news: " He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump's post read. He added, "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose." Trump noted that he thinks "streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die." That seemingly included Vice President JD Vance who said he wouldn't watch the execution. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) warned footage of the execution could become a "recruiting tool for future terrorists." Catch up quick: The Pentagon previously confirmed that the December execution would be streamed after Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice that it would be made "public." But the plan received swift pushback from Republicans and Democrats in Congress alike, as well as from clergy and survivors of the horrific 2009 attack. Even though most Americans support executing shooter Nidal Hasan, a vast majority oppose livestreaming his death by firing squad, according to a ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll out Thursday. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:a10a56e8f71f1acf.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Starlink satellite services are restored
33e1d7779a:a10a56e8f71f1acf.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:a10a56e8f71f1acf.summary: Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite services — critical tools in its war against Russia that were unexpectedly throttled this week — have been restored to full capacity, a Ukrainian official tells Axios. The official also said that Ukraine conducted a strike overnight against a Russian oil refinery — defying President Trump's demand that it stop hitting those facilities. Why it matters: The twin developments further strained the U.S.-Ukraine relationship, as the war with Russia drags on and the Trump administration sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week by lifting sanctions on Russian oil sales. State of play: The move angered Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky responded by calling it "a weak decision" and a "gift to Putin." Trump then called for Ukraine to elect a new president. The crisis intensified this week when Elon Musk's SpaceX restricted service of Starlink — a satellite service used for defensive purposes in battle — while Starshield, a tool used for offensive war operations that is controlled by the U.S. government, was also slowed. After more than a day, the services were restored. Ukraine, meanwhile, fired on a Russian oil refinery, which U.S. officials are unlikely to look kindly upon. The Ukrainian official said the country resumed strikes because Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump announcing that the two sides had agreed to a ceasefire. That declaration came as a surprise to Zelensky. The bottom line: It's still unclear to many inside the Trump administration and the Ukrainian government whether Trump ordered the satellite restrictions or not.

33e1d7779a:4056eadd6f688802.title: CEO confidence drops into negative territory
33e1d7779a:4056eadd6f688802.author: Emily Peck
33e1d7779a:4056eadd6f688802.summary: Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council; Chart: Axios/Emily Peck CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, finds a survey out Thursday morning from the Conference Board . Why it matters: Business leaders are mind-melding with most consumers, whose opinions on the economy are now lower than during the pandemic . Such sour sentiment is shaping up as a key issue in the midterms just weeks away. Where it stands: The CEO Confidence Index fell to 46 in the most recent period, down from 52 just three months ago — any number below 50 connotes negative sentiment. The nonprofit Conference Board and the Business Council surveyed 131 Fortune 500 CEOs from Sept. 21-Oct. 5. The survey measures how chief executives at major public companies feel about current economic conditions and their expectations for the economy and their own industries over the next six months. By the numbers: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter. Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago. 94% of CEOs cited cybersecurity threats among their top AI-related concerns. The surge in energy prices — particularly diesel, which is crucial to companies' energy costs — also contributed to the fall in sentiment, Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board, tells Axios. "All these inflationary shocks, one after the the other, is weighing down on the confidence of both CEOs and consumers," she says. Between the lines: The key worry when CEO moods darken is the spillover into the economy, as they pull back on spending and hiring. Reality check: Despite their dimming views, CEOs have for the most part maintained their spending plans, per the survey. Case in point: A separate survey also out Thursday morning found that 89% of U.S. CEOs said they expected to increase headcount over the next three years as AI creates more business opportunities. "As…

33e1d7779a:7279d0659ec1ebcd.title: YOLO Chuck: Schumer's final fight
33e1d7779a:7279d0659ec1ebcd.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:7279d0659ec1ebcd.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is on the cusp of leading his party to midterm victory and reclaiming his title as Senate majority leader. Winning the majority isn't guaranteed. But this son of Brooklyn, who has been in public life for 52 years, is more than favored to win a secret ballot to remain Democratic leader. Why it matters: At age 75 (76 by the time the new Congress convenes in January), Charles Ellis Schumer, an old-school pol who visits all 62 of New York's counties every year, looks poised to do what very few people do in life — go out on top. Behind the scenes: For starters, Democratic senators aren't quietly maneuvering — or publicly positioning themselves — to take the top job, according to senior aides. You can't beat someone with no one . A handful of Democratic Senate candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, haven't committed to supporting Schumer for leader. But they likely don't have the votes to stage a coup. And Schumer's super PAC is spending heavily to get them across the line. That calculus could change if Republicans overperform expectations with a massive win, potentially triggering a serious leadership challenge. Otherwise, the job is Schumer's for the asking — and he's asking. "I am running for re-election for leader. Period," he said two weeks ago. The intrigue: The bigger question surrounding Schumer involves 2028 and whether he'd retire at the top of his game or risk an embarrassing primary loss to, perhaps, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was born in the Bronx and represents parts of the Bronx and Queens. If Schumer decided to retire, he could spend his final two years in leadership, freed from the political pressures that have defined his career. That would give Senate Republicans and President Trump an entirely new political animal to contend with: YOLO Chuck. Republican YOLO senators (with nothing left to lose, since You Only Live Once) have been playing hardball with President…

33e1d7779a:4ded5238c4d1164b.title: Gen Z and millennials are running for Congress in record numbers, but few reach November
33e1d7779a:4ded5238c4d1164b.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:4ded5238c4d1164b.summary: Gen Z and millennials have launched their biggest bid yet to remake Congress, but roughly seven in 10 were out by early September, a new report finds. Why it matters: These two generations are struggling to clear the first hurdles of a political system that rewards experience, fundraising and established party support. State of play: A new report from Future Caucus , a nonpartisan nonprofit that works with younger elected officials, found that a record share of this cycle's congressional candidates came from the nation's two youngest political generations. The group identified 3,918 candidates who filed for Congress this cycle, 31% more than in 2024. Of candidates with known or estimated ages, 36.4% were millennials or Gen Z, up from 23.4% in 2024. The report counts everyone who filed and doesn't track how many were first-time candidates. Between the lines : Many young candidates are trying to reach Congress without the political experience that helps candidates advance. Just 1.7% of Gen Z candidates and 9% of millennials have served in a state legislature. Among congressional challengers with age data, nearly 40% of those with state legislative experience reached the general-election stage, compared with 26.2% without it. By the numbers: Only 21.2% of Gen Z congressional candidates remained in the race at the report's September cutoff. That figure rose to 30.2% for millennials, 41.1% for Gen X and 44.5% for Baby Boomers. Nearly 33% of Gen Z candidates failed to qualify for a primary ballot, compared with 18.3% of millennials and 9.4% of Gen X. Incumbents averaged 59 years old, nearly nine years older than challengers. What they're saying: "They're done waiting for somebody else to fix the problems," Future Caucus President and CEO Layla Zaidane tells Axios. Zaidane said Gen Z candidates running outside the two major parties face steep hurdles: raising money, recruiting volunteers and building name recognition without party infrastructure. Zoom in: Women make up…

33e1d7779a:b57f63159fa49b4f.title: America's not ready for the consequences of space warfare
33e1d7779a:b57f63159fa49b4f.author: Thomas Novelly
33e1d7779a:b57f63159fa49b4f.summary: The future of war is in outer space — and the U.S. is unprepared for the fallout. Why it matters: An outbreak of space warfare would cripple the global economy by disrupting satellites used for everything from worldwide financial transactions to maritime navigation. It would also hinder the U.S. military's ability to conduct some of its key missions on Earth. The dependence on satellites is precisely what makes them tempting targets for foes. China has made major advancements, such as satellites with robotic arms that could disable U.S. equipment and lasers that can blind military space sensors. Russia lags behind, but U.S. officials fear it may unleash an orbital nuclear weapon that "could pose a threat to all satellites and to the space-enabled services the world depends on." What they're saying: Todd Harrison, the American Enterprise Institute's space expert, said "we've been under the illusion" that an adversary would target only military satellites and leave civil or commercial ones alone. That's no longer the case. "In a future conflict, we could very well see the civilian and commercial space infrastructure that we often take for granted ... being attacked," Harrison said. "Is the American public ready for that? I'm not sure they are." " We're quickly coming to the conclusion that there's no sanctuary in space, not even in a small conflict," he added. Threat level: Last month, U.S. officials revealed that the military had weapons in space — a bombshell admission they said was aimed at deterring adversaries. Yes, but: Doug Loverro, a former top NASA and Pentagon space policy official, said the deterrence effect is "partially the case, but not really true." China and Russia have long assumed the U.S. has had space weapons, he said. In future wars, if adversaries feel they can't gain the upper hand against the U.S. military, infrastructure like GPS could be targeted, Loverro added. State of play: Aerospace analysts warn the nation isn't prepared if China or…

33e1d7779a:17b434413025b397.title: Anthropic brings Wall Street an AI bull case
33e1d7779a:17b434413025b397.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:17b434413025b397.summary: AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic on Wednesday made that case in cash. The company presented eye-popping financials to investors, saying it was cash flow positive in the third quarter, with revenue surging nearly 50% to $16.8 billion compared to the April-to-June period. Why it matters: As Wall Street broadly spent the day fearing an AI bubble, Anthropic offered what investors have been desperate to see: evidence that frontier AI can be a sustainable business . State of play: As concerns about the AI trade pushed the S&P 500 down by more than 1% for the first time in 53 sessions, Anthropic showed off a balance sheet that offered the promise of profitable AI, sources told Axios. Zoom in: Consider just one of the stats reported by Anthropic: the company is cash flow positive even as some of the world's most profitable companies are struggling to keep their AI spending in check. For context, Google parent Alphabet, long a money-printing machine, turned free cash flow negative in its second quarter as AI infrastructure investment soared. Investing gurus — especially those focused on the frothiness of companies relative to their underlying value — have long seen free cash flow as a gold standard for the long-term health of a business. Anthropic, a much younger company competing in the same expensive AI race, says it was cash flow positive in the third quarter. The Anthropic figures were first reported by the Financial Times . Yes, but : The company's blistering pace of growth appeared to slow compared to the difference between the first and second quarter, when sales more than doubled. Few investors saw growth as likely to continue at that pace, especially while the company faced ferocious competition from OpenAI. Between the lines: Anthropic's latest financial disclosures reinforce what analysts and investors have been telling Axios: The AI lab's early bets on frontier intelligence and…

33e1d7779a:66b5a48e727d53e3.title: Scoop: "OG" Bill Gates returns to wage war on AI risks
33e1d7779a:66b5a48e727d53e3.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:66b5a48e727d53e3.summary: Bill Gates is gearing up to dramatically expand his AI safety push , personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, sources tell Axios. Why it matters : The formidable, sharp-elbowed Bill Gates who built Microsoft is back, and he's directing his competitive fire toward what he has come to see as one of the most important causes of his lifetime. "I can reach CEOs on this better than you can," Gates told one person he consulted on AI safety, showing an eagerness for combat that associates say is a return to "OG" form. Driving the news : Once a voice for optimism on AI, Gates has grown dismayed by an escalation of model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as insufficient regulation, sources say. As he prepared to make the case for a far more robust regulatory framework on AI, he conferred extensively with leading AI executives, researchers, and safety advocates, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. That process led Gates to see containing AI risks as one of the most important issues he will engage with in his lifetime, the people said. Behind the scenes : People Gates has spoken to called his advocacy a "comeback tour," an attempt to rebuild a legacy that has been tarnished by his past association with Jeffrey Epstein. Gates has said he's aware that some people may dismiss his warnings due to the Epstein ties. "What I did do, in some ways, was very limited, and it was motivated by my desire to raise money," Gates told Axios in August. "But ... it was a huge mistake." However, Gates sees the stakes as too high to stay on the sidelines and believes his Rolodex, foundational tech credibility and wealth can do an immense amount of good. The big picture : This crusade marks a stark evolution for Gates, moving him from a measured optimist to an urgent alarmist. Just three years ago, Gates assured the public that "the risks of AI are real but manageable." He viewed the technology's disruptions as…

33e1d7779a:da84747dda7be703.title: Scoop: Inside Elon Musk's massive Texas rescue mission
33e1d7779a:da84747dda7be703.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:da84747dda7be703.summary: Elon Musk 's team reached out to Republicans in late August to discuss a train wreck they all saw coming: Unless the GOP poured more money into Texas immediately, the state's Senate race could be lost in a matter of weeks. Why it matters: That chat set in motion a massive rescue operation for Republican Ken Paxton funded substantially by Musk, the party's largest donor, who gave $158 million in September alone. Musk's rescue gave Paxton's sleepy campaign new life and showed why the world's richest person is the X factor in the push to prevent a midterm debacle for President Trump's party. Zoom out: It also helped Republicans avoid a death-spiral scenario: that propping up Paxton in Texas would force them to drain badly needed resources from other Senate battlegrounds. Instead, Musk's money allowed Republicans to flood Texas' expensive TV markets and free up cash to shore up unexpectedly competitive races in Kansas and South Carolina . Behind the scenes: In late August, Democrat James Talarico was dominating the Texas airwaves, portraying Paxton, the state's attorney general, as one of the nation's most corrupt politicians. Paxton, who isn't known as a prolific fundraiser, was dark on TV. Polling seen by Musk's team and the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) suggested his chances were sinking. Against that backdrop, Musk's top political adviser, Chris Young, called SLF president Alex Latcham with an idea: Musk would donate $5 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC if that group raised another $5 million. Latcham countered: Would Musk contribute $10 million if the pro-Paxton group raised $5 million and SLF put up another $5 million? Young agreed. Within days, Republicans had mobilized $20 million to get Paxton on TV. The intrigue: That was just the beginning. SLF and Musk's America PAC concluded that a much larger operation was needed, given the enormous cost of advertising in Texas. SLF and the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. would air tens of millions of dollars in pro-Paxton ads,…

33e1d7779a:706ad4e62b7672b4.title: Scoop: The FTC demanded documents from AI giants over recent safety incidents
33e1d7779a:706ad4e62b7672b4.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:706ad4e62b7672b4.summary: The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday sent civil subpoenas to AI giants seeking documents about safety incidents that have spiraled into an industry crisis . The FTC sought documents from Anthropic and OpenAI with the scope of the probe focused on potential consumer protection violations, a person familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The investigation is one of a number of steps the administration has taken to show a firm hand with AI companies after multiple incidents in which unreleased models hacked websites or took deceptive or aggressive steps in testing. State of play: The agency on Wednesday sent out civil investigative demands, which help the government gather evidence and investigate ahead of potential litigation. They are more than 50 pages long each and ask for documents concerning security incidents and safeguarding practices. The agency is also asking for marketing materials and documents detailing company privacy policies, the source said. Investigative demands will be sent to third party AI organizations at a later date, the person familiar said. Zoom in: The FTC has plans to compel top AI executives to testify about their products, according to the source. The agency has investigative authority to examine actions related to consumer harms that could be seen as unfair or deceptive. Those can relate to a wide range of misbehavior, from how companies charge for services or if they're alleged to have misled users. AI companies continue to face scrutiny about the safety of their products. Ferguson has echoed the view of other administration figures and executives that AI systems shouldn't be released if they aren't safe. OpenAI faces a litany of lawsuits. A group of state attorneys general on Wednesday sued OpenAI under consumer protection laws for allegedly misleading users, including children, on the safety of its chatbot. The big picture: The Trump administration has taken on a more aggressive posture toward AI companies as safety incident…

33e1d7779a:ba9b1f0db392c8d2.title: Unexpected House battles pop up deep in Trump country
33e1d7779a:ba9b1f0db392c8d2.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:ba9b1f0db392c8d2.summary: Republicans who haven't faced serious reelection fights in years are suddenly campaigning like they're running in swing districts. Why it matters: Democrats are eyeing House districts so Republican that they weren't even on the party's radar at the start of the 2026 midterm election cycle. That includes incumbents like Reps. John McGuire (R-Va.) and Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), neither of whom were seen as remotely vulnerable coming into the second Trump term. Most of these seats haven't elected a Democrat in years or even decades and are only truly in play if the party is winning nationally by double digits. Even then, some are a stretch. But candidates in Trump country say frustration with rising prices, corruption, the war in Iran and political incumbency in general have led to a sea change that could precipitate some shock results on Nov. 3. State of play: Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Mich.) is running scathing attack ads against Democratic opponent Callie Barr, labeling her "Crooked Callie" and tying her to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib and Abdul El-Sayed. That's a stark change from 2024, when Bergman defeated Barr by 21 percentage points. His ads that cycle made at most a passing reference to Barr , according to AdImpact. Rep. John McGuire (R-Va.) won by 15 points in 2024, a sleepy general election with minimal spending or ads. He too is running attack ads amid a challenge from former Democratic Rep. Tom Perriello. What we're hearing: Democrats say they are astounded by the level of anti-establishment frustration in their districts. "We're in a real race. It's unreal," Barr said in an interview, telling Axios voters regularly come to her campaign offices "just to vent their frustration" with the incumbent. "I ran in '24, and I can see, in real time, the shift," she said. "I mean, look at the commercial Jack Bergman ran about me. There's a track behind it that's whispering, 'lies.'" Richard Ojeda, who is running against National Republican Congressional…

33e1d7779a:5cc2215434da04b8.title: Republicans brace for three-way leader fight if they lose
33e1d7779a:5cc2215434da04b8.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:5cc2215434da04b8.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson's sudden frank talk about his political future is upending the quiet maneuvering ahead of a post-election GOP leadership contest. Why it matters: The race could become a three-way fight if Johnson follows former Speaker Nancy Pelosi's example and tries to stay in leadership if Republicans lose the majority. Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) has widely been viewed as a top contender for the job — and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) did not seek a waiver to remain Judiciary chair, fueling speculation that he's preparing to run for leader. Many Republicans privately worry they're going to lose and expected Johnson to step aside if the majority slips away. But his new blunt and unexpected musings on his own future challenge that assumption. Driving the news: "In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News. But some members aren't buying it: "Why would you want to be minority leader after speaker?" one House Republican told us, adding they would support new leadership. One leader not taking the bait is Scalise: "There are no races that any of us need to be talking about until after the election's over," he told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning out west. Scalise acknowledged Johnson's comments: "I think early on he said he wasn't going to play in hypotheticals, and you know, and he might have gone down that path for a minute. We're focused on holding the House, and that's where my energy is." Between the lines: A bad enough defeat could spark calls for an entirely new leadership team, three House Republicans told us. But Johnson has his defenders: "Johnson has done everything humanly possible to keep us in the majority," one House Republican told Axios. Zoom in: Some GOP sources believe a three-way contest could split support between Johnson and Scalise, potentially benefiting Jordan.…

33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.title: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.summary: The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia. Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When it doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Service was partially restored on Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible. The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president. A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious. Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night. The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph. The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries. U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration. "We had massive [Russian] attacks today and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the top of…

33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.summary: AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers. Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them. Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI. Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from." Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit . Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room." Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved. The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded. The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes. Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in…

33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.title: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.summary: The Trump administration is threatening emergency court action unless California officials investigate potential ineligible voters within 48 hours and set aside ballots from anyone whose citizenship they cannot verify, according to two letters sent to state officials from the Justice Department. Why it matters: With voting already underway, President Trump 's DOJ could delay ballots from eligible Californians mistakenly flagged as noncitizens and set up a court fight just three weeks before Election Day. Driving the news: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent a letter Tuesday to Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan along with a thumb drive of "likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot," according to a copy of the letter shared with Axios. McCotter asks local officials to investigate their citizenship status by noon October 15. The letter did not say how many people are on the list. For anyone whose status can't be confirmed, DOJ asks the officials to "segregate—not cancel" those ballots and suspend signature verification or counting of any ballots already returned. DOJ also asks officials to withhold ballots from people on the list unless their citizenship has been confirmed. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber received a similar letter . Friction point: McCotter closed his letter with a threat: "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief." What they're saying: "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. The California secretary of state's office and the Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment. The other side: "One must question…

33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.title: ICE says no to automatic body-cams
33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.summary: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs amid shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back,…

33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.summary: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.title: New inflation warning sign
33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.summary: America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy . Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further. What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note. The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote. By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month. Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%. The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening. Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge. Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs. "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months. The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest…

33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.summary: Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter. That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month. The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax. How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment. Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January. However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years. The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

33e1d7779a:8126cc7715c56735.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures…

33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.summary: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped…

ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.title: More than just Plug and Play: Early Evidence on Organisational Capital and AI Adoption
ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.author: Riley, Rebecca
ecbefe1924:8cf67b22b6800fad.summary: This paper provides early evidence that AI adoption by firms is linked to management practices in unique ways. Using panel data from the UK Management and Expectations Survey (MES), we find that firms with higher baseline management scores are significantly more likely to adopt AI. This relationship is specific to AI: the same management practices show no relationship with the adoption of other technologies such as robotics, specialized equipment, or specialized software. We also find that management capabilities related to performance measurement appear strongly related to AI adoption. These results suggest that organisational complementarities are specific to different technologies, with implications for policies to encourage AI adoption by firms.

ecbefe1924:8eba6c7514699b63.title: Wage growth of less educated workers: the importance of social skills
ecbefe1924:8eba6c7514699b63.author: Griffith, Rachel
ecbefe1924:8eba6c7514699b63.summary: We use matched employee–employer data from the UK to investigate the importance of social skills – in particular, teamwork and communication with co-workers – as a driver of wage growth for workers with lower formal education. We find that in social skill tasks, a significant fraction of less educated workers enjoy wage progression with tenure, and higher returns in firms with more educated co-workers. We rationalise these dynamics through a model in which social skills – initially opaque to both employee and employer – are learned about over time through complementarity with co-workers.

ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.title: Beyond the Paycheck: Using Fringe Benefits to Attract a Broader Pool of Applicants
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.author: Thea S. Zoellner
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.summary: Many firms in tight labor markets recruit for highly gender-segregated occupations, leaving them, in effect, drawing from only half the potential labor pool. We study how firms can use fringe benefits to attract workers and influence occupational choice. Unlike occupation-specific recruiting strategies, fringe benefits can be added to any occupation; they are also easily tailored, implemented, and scaled. Using a personalized and incentivized discrete choice experiment, we present participants with job options that match their skills and work task preferences. Within each option, we vary salary, occupation, and fringe benefits that adolescents had classified as gender-neutral, male-typed, or female-typed. We find that fringe benefits are highly valued: their effect is around a third as large as having prior interest in the occupation. Neutral and stereotypical benefits in particular improve perceptions of the firm across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we find substantial gender differences. Female-typed benefits deter male participants, whereas all other benefit-participant combinations have a positive effect. Female participants value benefits more when those benefits are paired with an atypical occupation, and we find suggestive evidence that this reflects benefits alleviating concerns about limited support in such roles. In addition, male-typed benefits can increase the attractiveness of gender-atypical occupations for female participants. Female participants who consider atypical occupations place relatively higher value on these benefits and tend to exhibit less traditionally feminine preferences. We also find suggestive evidence that anticipated social reactions, particularly from parents, accompany these choices.

ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.title: How to Increase the Mental Well-Being of Your Employees? An Overview of Research Testing Interventions in the Workplace
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.author: Baert, Stijn
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.summary: This systematic literature review provides a state-of-the-art overview of the effectiveness of workplace interventions aimed at improving workersâ€™ mental well-being. Specifically, it examines which types of interventions are effective for which aspects of mental well-being, both in the short and long term. To this end, we identify 125 randomised controlled trials comprising 147 interventions that vary in their objectives (prevention, treatment, or reintegration), targets (workers or work), methods (cognitive, meditation-based, physical, ergonomic, organisational, or multimethod) and delivery channels (offline, online or hybrid). Mental well-being outcomes are classified as biological and self-reported indicators of the three components of subjective mental well-being (evaluative, affective, and eudaimonic well-being). Overall, we find that, for preventing and treating early mental health symptoms, cognitive or meditation-based interventions targeting personal coping resources appear most promising. In contrast, successful reintegration seems to require a combination of cognitive and organisational interventions, with the latter addressing job demands and resources.

ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.title: Meetings
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.author: Yaling Xu
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.summary: Why do we have so many meetings? Few workplace features are so scorned, yet seemingly so necessary. This paper provides the first large-scale economic evidence on workplace meetings using an original survey of more than 9, 000 workers linked to matched employer–employee administrative data from Norway. We show that meetings are both common and costly, consuming an average of 12 percent of work hours and 14 percent of firm wage bills. Planning, problem solving, information sharing, and project coordination account for the majority of meeting activity. High-paying and high-revenue firms devote more resources to meetings despite facing a substantially higher opportunity cost of employee time. Meeting frequency and intensity are positively related to worker wage growth. Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism. Meetings are the broccoli of work – widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.
